question: A 55-year-old man presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting for 24 hours. On examination he has epigastric tenderness with guarding. His ALT is 142 U/L, AST 118 U/L, bilirubin 58 umol/L, ALP 210 U/L, and amylase 1840 U/L. Per NICE guidance, what are the two most likely diagnoses to consider?

options.B: Acute pancreatitis (amylase >1000 U/L = highly significant) AND cholestasis/biliary obstruction (raised bilirubin, ALP, transaminases) — gallstone pancreatitis is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis in the UK, accounting for 50% of cases

explanation.correct: Acute pancreatitis: severe epigastric pain radiating to the back + vomiting + markedly raised amylase (>1000 U/L — very high specificity when >3× upper limit of normal). The raised LFTs (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin) point to biliary/cholestatic component — strongly suggesting gallstone pancreatitis (gallstone impacted at ampulla of Vater causing both biliary obstruction and pancreatic duct obstruction). Gallstones account for ~50% of acute pancreatitis in the UK; alcohol ~25%. Per UK guidelines (BSG 2005): USS abdomen within 24 hours to identify gallstones; MRCP or EUS if USS inconclusive; severity assessment using Modified Glasgow/Ranson/APACHE-II or CRP; ERCP within 72 hours if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Peptic ulcer and hepatitis do not cause an amylase of 1840 U/L.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acute pancreatitis (amylase >1000) + cholestatic pattern LFTs = gallstone pancreatitis in UK primary care context per BSG guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Appendicitis causes RIF pain and does not cause amylase >1000 U/L.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cirrhosis and encephalopathy have a different clinical and biochemical picture.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Mesenteric ischaemia causes bowel necrosis with different biochemistry.

reference: BSG — Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines 2005. NICE CKS — Pancreatitis. https://www.bsg.org.uk/clinical-resource/bsg-guidelines-management-acute-pancreatitis/

question: A 48-year-old woman is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Per the Modified Glasgow Scoring System, which five parameters are used to assess severity at 48 hours?

options.B: PaO2 <8 kPa, albumin <32 g/L, urea >16 mmol/L, glucose >10 mmol/L (non-diabetic), LDH >600 U/L, AST/ALT >200 U/L, calcium <2.0 mmol/L, WBC >15 × 10⁹/L — score ≥3 at 48 hours = severe pancreatitis — mnemonic PANCREAS
options.C: HR, RR, BP, temperature, GCS only
options.D: CRP >150 mg/L alone indicates severity at 48 hours
options.E: Amylase level determines severity — >5000 U/L = severe

explanation.correct: The Modified Glasgow Score (Imrie Score) uses 8 parameters measured at 48 hours post-onset — mnemonic PANCREAS: PaO2 <8 kPa; Age >55 years; Neutrophils (WBC >15 × 10⁹/L); Calcium <2.0 mmol/L; Renal (urea >16 mmol/L); Enzymes (LDH >600 U/L, AST/ALT >200 U/L); Albumin <32 g/L; Sugar (glucose >10 mmol/L in non-diabetics). Score ≥3 at 48 hours = severe acute pancreatitis requiring HDU/ICU admission. CRP >150 mg/L at 48 hours is an independent marker of severity per BSG guidelines. Importantly, the amylase level at diagnosis does NOT predict severity — it can be normal in severe necrotising pancreatitis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — These are not the Glasgow score parameters.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Modified Glasgow (PANCREAS) score ≥3 at 48 hours = severe acute pancreatitis per BSG guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — These are general clinical parameters — not the Glasgow pancreatitis severity score.
explanation.D: Incorrect — CRP >150 is a severity marker but the Glasgow score uses 8 specific parameters.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Amylase level does NOT predict pancreatitis severity — severity is determined by Glasgow score/CRP at 48 hours.

reference: BSG — Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines. Modified Glasgow Score. https://www.bsg.org.uk/clinical-resource/bsg-guidelines-management-acute-pancreatitis/

question: A 42-year-old man presents with a 3-hour history of severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. He drinks 40 units of alcohol per week. His serum amylase is 1,650 U/L. Per NICE CKS and BSG guidance, what is the immediate primary care management?

options.A: Prescribe oral omeprazole and review in 48 hours
options.B: 999 / immediate A&E transfer — acute pancreatitis is a potentially life-threatening surgical emergency requiring IV fluids, analgesia, nutritional support and monitoring for complications (necrosis, abscess, ARDS, multi-organ failure)
options.C: Prescribe oral amoxicillin for infective pancreatitis
options.D: Arrange outpatient USS and review in 1 week
options.E: Admit for bed rest and clear fluids only

explanation.correct: Acute pancreatitis is a potentially life-threatening emergency requiring immediate hospital admission. Mortality: mild cases ~1%, severe necrotising pancreatitis up to 30-40%. Immediate primary care management: 999 / direct A&E admission. Hospital management per BSG: (1) IV fluid resuscitation (Hartmann's solution preferred — reduces CRP and systemic inflammation); (2) Analgesia (IV/IM opioids); (3) Monitoring (fluid balance, electrolytes, blood glucose, oxygen saturation); (4) NBM initially then early enteral feeding if tolerated (nasojejunal if severe); (5) USS within 24 hours for aetiology (gallstones?); (6) Severity assessment (Glasgow score at 48 hours); (7) Consider HDU/ICU if severe. Routine antibiotics are NOT indicated for uncomplicated pancreatitis — only for confirmed infected necrosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PPI alone for acute pancreatitis is dangerously inadequate — immediate hospital admission is essential.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Acute pancreatitis: 999/immediate A&E for IV fluids, analgesia, monitoring and severity assessment per BSG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Outpatient USS in 1 week while the patient has acute pancreatitis risks missed severe disease and organ failure.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 'Bed rest and clear fluids' alone in primary care is insufficient — IV fluids, analgesia and monitoring in hospital are required.

reference: BSG — Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines 2005. NICE CKS — Pancreatitis. https://www.bsg.org.uk/

question: A 28-year-old woman has been diagnosed with a first episode of mild-moderate ulcerative colitis (UC) affecting the left colon. Per NICE NG130, what is the first-line treatment to induce remission?

options.B: Topical mesalazine suppository (proctitis) or mesalazine enema (left-sided colitis) — topical 5-ASA (aminosalicylate) is first-line for mild-moderate distal/left-sided UC to induce remission; combined oral + topical mesalazine is more effective than either alone for extensive or resistant disease
options.C: Infliximab (anti-TNF) — biologic first-line for all UC
options.D: Methotrexate — standard disease-modifying agent for UC
options.E: Ciprofloxacin — antibiotics for UC remission induction

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG130 (Ulcerative colitis: management), treatment of mild-moderate UC is stratified by extent: Proctitis (rectum only): topical mesalazine suppository 1g daily — first-line; Distal/left-sided colitis: topical mesalazine enema (1-2g daily) ± oral mesalazine; Extensive colitis: combined oral + topical mesalazine or oral mesalazine alone. Oral prednisolone (40mg daily reducing over 8 weeks) is reserved for: failure of topical therapy, moderate-severe disease, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Azathioprine/mercaptopurine are for maintenance of steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing UC — not induction. Biologics (infliximab, vedolizumab, tofacitinib) are for moderate-severe UC refractory to conventional therapy. Methotrexate is NOT used in UC (unlike Crohn's disease).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral prednisolone is second-line for left-sided mild-moderate UC — topical mesalazine is first-line per NICE NG130.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Topical mesalazine (enema for left-sided UC) is first-line for mild-moderate distal UC per NICE NG130.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Anti-TNF biologics are for moderate-severe UC refractory to conventional therapy — not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Methotrexate is not used in UC (it is used in Crohn's disease). Azathioprine is used in UC for maintenance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Antibiotics are not standard remission induction therapy for UC.

reference: NICE NG130 — Ulcerative colitis: management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130

question: A 32-year-old man with ulcerative colitis is in remission after topical mesalazine. Per NICE NG130, what maintenance treatment should be offered to prevent relapse?

options.A: No maintenance treatment — stop mesalazine once remission is achieved
options.B: Oral mesalazine (low-dose maintenance) or topical mesalazine — long-term 5-ASA maintenance is recommended for UC to prevent relapse; treatment should be continued indefinitely
options.C: Oral prednisolone indefinitely — steroid maintenance prevents UC relapse
options.E: Mesalazine only during symptomatic flares — no continuous maintenance needed

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG130, all patients with UC who have achieved remission should be offered long-term maintenance therapy with oral mesalazine (or topical mesalazine for proctitis). 5-ASA maintenance: reduces relapse rate by ~50%; is well-tolerated with low side effects; should be continued indefinitely as stopping leads to high relapse rates. Oral steroids (prednisolone) must NOT be used for long-term maintenance — they cause significant systemic adverse effects without sustained remission benefit. If UC patient relapses ≥2 times per year on mesalazine, or is steroid-dependent: add azathioprine or mercaptopurine for maintenance. Annual colonoscopic surveillance is required for UC patients from 8-10 years after extensive disease onset (cancer surveillance).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Stopping mesalazine after achieving remission significantly increases relapse risk — maintenance therapy should continue indefinitely.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Long-term oral/topical mesalazine maintenance is recommended to prevent UC relapse per NICE NG130.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Long-term prednisolone for UC maintenance is NOT recommended — adverse effects are significant and it does not achieve sustained remission.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Infliximab maintenance is for moderate-severe UC refractory to 5-ASA and immunomodulators — not for mild-moderate UC in remission.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Continuous maintenance (not just during flares) is the evidence-based approach per NICE NG130.

reference: NICE NG130 — Ulcerative colitis: management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130

question: A 35-year-old man with Crohn's disease has an acute flare with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and CRP 68 mg/L. Per NICE NG129, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment to induce remission in Crohn's disease?

options.A: Topical mesalazine — same as ulcerative colitis
options.B: Oral prednisolone 40mg daily tapering over 8 weeks — corticosteroids are first-line for inducing remission in Crohn's disease; budesonide (9mg daily) is an alternative for ileocaecal Crohn's with fewer systemic side effects
options.D: Infliximab as first-line for all Crohn's

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG129 (Crohn's disease: management), first-line treatment to induce remission in Crohn's disease: oral prednisolone 40mg daily reducing over 8 weeks, OR budesonide 9mg daily for 8 weeks (ileocaecal Crohn's — fewer systemic effects due to first-pass hepatic metabolism). Key distinction from UC: mesalazine (5-ASA) is NOT effective for inducing remission in Crohn's disease (unlike UC) — this is a high-yield AKT distinction. Azathioprine/mercaptopurine are maintenance agents (prevent relapse) — not induction agents. Biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) are for moderate-severe Crohn's refractory to conventional immunomodulators. Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, metronidazole) are used for perianal Crohn's disease — not routine induction.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Mesalazine/5-ASA is NOT effective for inducing remission in Crohn's disease — this is a key AKT distinction from UC.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Prednisolone 40mg (or budesonide for ileocaecal disease) is first-line induction for Crohn's per NICE NG129.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Azathioprine is a maintenance agent (prevents relapse) — not used for acute induction of remission.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Anti-TNF biologics are reserved for moderate-severe Crohn's refractory to conventional therapy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Antibiotics are used specifically for perianal/fistulating Crohn's — not routine induction therapy.

reference: NICE NG129 — Crohn's disease: management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129

question: A 38-year-old woman with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) has had normal colonoscopy, coeliac serology and thyroid function. She has ongoing abdominal pain, bloating and alternating bowel habit. First-line lifestyle and dietary measures have been tried. Per NICE CG61, what is the first-line pharmacological option for IBS with persistent symptoms?

options.B: Antispasmodics (hyoscine butylbromide, mebeverine, peppermint oil) for abdominal pain/cramps; loperamide for diarrhoea-predominant; low-dose amitriptyline (10-30mg nocte) as second-line for pain when antispasmodics fail — amitriptyline is specifically recommended by NICE CG61 for IBS refractory to first-line measures
options.E: Immediate colonoscopy — repeat investigation if treatment fails

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG61 (Irritable bowel syndrome in adults), the management hierarchy: (1) Dietary/lifestyle: regular meals, reduced insoluble fibre, reduced caffeine/alcohol/fizzy drinks, adequate fluid; (2) Antispasmodics (mebeverine 135mg TDS, hyoscine 10-20mg QDS, or peppermint oil) for cramping pain; loperamide 2-4mg PRN for diarrhoea; ispaghula husk for constipation; (3) Second-line: tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline 10mg nocte — low dose; titrate to 30-50mg if needed) for persistent pain, not responding to antispasmodics; SSRIs if amitriptyline not tolerated; (4) Psychological therapies (CBT, hypnotherapy, psychotherapy) for severe or refractory IBS. Note: the question recall specifically states 'amitriptyline' as the answer for IBS with normal investigations — NICE CG61 endorses this as second-line.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Prednisolone is not used in IBS — there is no inflammatory pathology.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Antispasmodics first-line for pain; amitriptyline second-line for refractory IBS per NICE CG61.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Metronidazole is not standard IBS treatment — bacterial overgrowth is a separate diagnosis requiring SIBO breath test confirmation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PPIs treat GORD/peptic ulcer — not IBS symptoms.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Repeat colonoscopy is not indicated in confirmed IBS with normal initial investigations and absence of new red flags.

reference: NICE CG61 — Irritable bowel syndrome in adults. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg61
